points.answer: Esau expresses amazement that Jacob was given a name that foreshadowed his destiny to supplant others, implying the name was prophetically given.

points.q: According to Rashi's Midrash, why was Isaac trembling before he even knew the truth?
options: He was worried he had sinned by blessing the younger before the elder and violating the proper order
He was cold and hungry
He was afraid of Esau's anger
points.kasha: What spiritual concern caused Isaac's trembling before he discovered the deception?
points.answer: Isaac feared he had overstepped the bounds of justice by blessing Jacob, the younger, before Esau, the elder—reversing the proper order of succession.

points.q: How does Rashi explain the meaning of 'ויעקבני' (he supplanted me)?
options: He lay in wait for me or outwitted me, showing cunning and deception
He hit me on the heel
He stole my inheritance documents
points.kasha: What is the precise meaning of the word 'ויעקבני' that Esau uses?
points.answer: Rashi interprets it as 'and he lay in wait for me' or 'he outwitted me'—meaning Jacob used cleverness and cunning to deceive him.

points.q: What does Rashi explain the word 'אצלת' (hast thou not reserved) means?
options: Separating or setting aside
Hiding or concealing
Blessing or sanctifying
points.kasha: The word אצלת appears in Esau's question to his father, and its meaning needs clarification.
points.answer: Rashi explains that אצלת means 'separating' or 'setting aside,' similar to the word 'ויאצל' (and he separated) used elsewhere in Scripture.

points.q: Why does Isaac emphasize that he made Jacob a master over Esau when responding to Esau's request for a blessing?
options: To show that any blessing Jacob receives will benefit him, not Esau, since a servant's acquisitions belong to the master
To prove that he loves Jacob more than Esau
To explain that Jacob has already received all the blessings
points.kasha: Isaac seems to be giving Esau a seventh blessing, yet he emphasizes Jacob's mastery over him—what is the connection?
points.answer: Rashi explains that Isaac is telling Esau that even if a blessing were given to him, it would be useless, because whatever property Esau acquires as a servant would legally belong to Jacob, his master.

points.q: What does Rashi clarify about Isaac's rhetorical question 'What shall I do now for you'?
options: It expresses where or how Isaac can find something else to do for Esau
It shows Isaac's frustration with Esau's demands
It means Isaac will do nothing more for Esau
points.kasha: The phrase 'ולכה אפוא מה אעשה' (and what shall I do now) requires understanding of the word 'אפוא' (where).
points.answer: Rashi explains that 'אפוא' means 'where,' so Isaac is asking: where shall I look for something else to do for you?

points.q: What grammatical function does the letter ה serve in the word 'הברכה' in Esau's question?
options: It is the interrogative prefix, expressing a question
It is a definite article making the word 'the blessing'
It is a suffix indicating possession
points.kasha: The phrase 'הברכה אחת' (hast thou but one blessing) needs grammatical clarification to understand what Esau is asking.
points.answer: Rashi explains that the ה is the interrogative prefix expressing a question, similar to how it functions in other biblical phrases like 'הבמחנים' (whether in camps) or 'השמנה' (whether it is fat).

points.q: What geographical location does Rashi identify when Isaac says Esau's dwelling will be 'from the fatness of the earth'?
options: The Greek portions of Italy (Magna Graecia)
The land of Egypt
The mountainous regions of Edom
points.kasha: The phrase 'משמני הארץ' (the fatness of the earth) in Isaac's blessing to Esau refers to a specific location that needs identification.
points.answer: Rashi identifies this as referring to Graecia Magna—the Greek portions of Italy—where Esau's descendants would eventually settle.

points.q: What grammatical substitution does Rashi identify with the word 'על' (on/by) in 'ועל חרבך' (and by thy sword)?
options: The word 'על' is used instead of the prefix 'ב' (by/with)
The word 'על' means 'above' in this context
The word 'על' is a preposition indicating proximity
points.kasha: The phrase 'ועל חרבך' uses 'על' in a way that seems unusual and requires grammatical clarification.
points.answer: Rashi explains that 'על' here substitutes for the prefix 'ב,' so the phrase means 'by your sword,' with biblical parallels showing similar usage in other verses.

points.q: What emotion or state does the word 'תריד' (shall grow restive) express, according to Rashi?
options: Grief or pain, referring to distress about lost blessings
Physical restlessness or agitation
Rebellion or political uprising
points.kasha: The meaning of 'תריד' in the phrase 'כאשר תריד' (when thou rovest about) needs clarification.
points.answer: Rashi explains that 'תריד' signifies grief or pain, meaning when Israel transgresses the Torah and Esau has reason to feel aggrieved about the blessings Jacob received, then he will break Jacob's yoke.

points.q: According to Rashi, why does Esau say 'the days of mourning for my father approach' before killing Jacob?
options: To avoid causing grief to his father Isaac while he is still alive
Because he wants to inherit his father's estate first
Because the mourning period will give him a legal justification
points.kasha: Esau's statement about his father's mourning period seems to interrupt his threat to kill Jacob, requiring explanation of his intent.
points.answer: Rashi explains according to the plain meaning that Esau will wait until after his father's death to kill Jacob, so as not to cause grief to Isaac while he is still alive.

points.q: According to Rashi, how did Rebekah know what Esau was thinking in his heart?
options: It was told to her by the Holy Spirit
She overheard Esau speaking to his servants
Isaac revealed Esau's thoughts to her
points.kasha: The verse says words were reported to Rebekah, but it doesn't explain how she learned Esau's private intentions
points.answer: Rashi explains that the Holy Spirit revealed to Rebekah what Esau was contemplating in his heart, indicating she had prophetic knowledge of his murderous thoughts.

points.q: What does Rashi say the phrase 'consoling himself' means in this context?
options: Esau is comforting himself by planning to compensate for his lost blessings through killing Jacob
Esau is genuinely grieving and needs emotional support
Esau is rejoicing with his friends over a recent victory
points.kasha: The phrase 'consoling himself' seems odd when describing someone planning a murder, requiring explanation of what he is actually consoling himself about
points.answer: Rashi explains that Esau is consoling himself for the loss of the blessings by deciding to kill Jacob—this act of vengeance will comfort him for what he lost.

points.q: What does Rashi say the word 'ahadim' (אחדים) means?
options: A few days
Many days
One specific day
points.kasha: The Hebrew word אחדים requires clarification of its meaning to understand how long Jacob should stay with Laban
points.answer: Rashi defines אחדים as meaning a small number of days—i.e., 'a few.'

points.q: What does Rashi explain the word 'shakol' (שכל) means in this verse?
options: To be bereaved of children through death
To be separated from one's children temporarily
To inherit property from one's children
points.kasha: The unusual verb form 'ashkal' needs explanation to understand what loss Rebekah fears
points.answer: Rashi explains that 'shakol' means to be bereaved—one who buries his children is called 'shkul,' and he cites Jacob's later use of the same word to illustrate this meaning.

points.q: According to Rashi, why does Rebekah fear losing both sons in one day?
options: The Holy Spirit revealed to her that if Jacob kills Esau in self-defense, Esau's sons will kill Jacob
She simply worries that Jacob might get sick traveling to Laban
She fears that both will decide to leave her household forever
points.kasha: It is unclear why sending Jacob away to escape Esau would result in losing both sons on one day
points.answer: Rashi explains that the Holy Spirit revealed to Rebekah a prophecy that if Jacob kills Esau in a fight, Esau's children will rise up and kill Jacob—thus both would die on the same day.

points.q: What does Rashi say the phrase 'qatzti b'chayai' means?
options: I am disgusted with my life
I am cutting short my life
I am hastening toward my death
points.kasha: The Hebrew phrase קצתי בחיי is somewhat ambiguous and requires explanation of its precise meaning
points.answer: Rashi explains that קצתי בחיי means 'I am disgusted with my life' or 'I loathe my life.'

points.q: What grammatical form does Rashi identify for the word 'Padnah'?
options: It is equivalent to 'l'Paddan' (to Padan) with the prefix 'l'
It is a different place name with no connection to Paddan
It is a dual form meaning two regions
points.kasha: The spelling 'Padnah' appears unusual and its relationship to the fuller name 'Paddan-aram' is unclear
points.answer: Rashi explains that פדנה is the same as לפדן (l'Paddan), showing that the 'h' ending serves the same function as a 'l' prefix.

points.q: According to Rashi, what grammatical principle explains the spelling 'beyitah' in this verse?
options: Words normally requiring a 'l' prefix can instead take an 'h' suffix
The 'h' suffix indicates a feminine noun
The 'h' suffix shows a diminutive form
points.kasha: The phrase 'beyitah Betu'el' (ביתה בתואל) appears to have an unusual 'h' ending rather than expected prepositions
points.answer: Rashi explains that any word requiring a 'l' prefix at its beginning can instead have an 'h' attached as a suffix, so 'beyitah' serves the same function as 'l'beyit' (to the house).

points.q: What does Rashi explain the name 'El Shaddai' to mean?
options: He who has a sufficiency of blessings for those who receive His blessing
He who is mighty and powerful over all creation
He who appears in dreams and visions to the righteous
points.kasha: The verse uses the name 'El Shaddai' but its meaning is not immediately clear from the text.
points.answer: Rashi explains that 'Shaddai' means He who has a sufficiency (dai) of blessings for those who are blessed by Him—emphasizing God's abundance of blessing.

points.q: What does Rashi mean when he says the blessings 'have been said regarding you'?
options: That the same blessings promised to Abraham should now apply to Jacob
That Jacob must recite the same blessings Abraham did each day
That the blessings were literally written down for Jacob to read
points.kasha: The verse mentions giving Jacob 'the blessing of Abraham,' but it's not clear what specific blessings that refers to.
points.answer: Rashi clarifies that the blessings God promised Abraham—becoming a great nation and having all nations blessed through his seed—should now be transferred to and fulfilled through Jacob.

points.q: What does Rashi's comment about this phrase reveal about his approach to interpretation?
options: He admits he doesn't know what purpose these words serve in the text
He explains a hidden meaning only the wise can understand
He corrects an error in the Torah's phrasing
points.kasha: The verse identifies Rebekah as 'mother of Jacob and Esau,' which seems redundant since their relationship is already established.
points.answer: Rashi honestly acknowledges that he does not know what the addition of these particular words is meant to teach us.

points.q: According to Rashi, how should we read the sequence of events in verses 6-7?
options: As a connected narrative explaining why Esau went to Ishmael: because Jacob obeyed his father and left
As separate stories with no connection between Jacob's obedience and Esau's actions
As a flashback showing Jacob's obedience before the blessing occurred
points.kasha: The verse begins a new sentence about Jacob hearkening, but it seems to connect to Esau's observation in the previous verse, making the flow unclear.
points.answer: Rashi explains that verse 7 ('Jacob hearkened') should be connected back to verse 6 about Esau seeing, so that Esau's decision to go to Ishmael is directly prompted by seeing that Jacob obeyed his father and went to Padan-aram.

points.q: Why does Rashi need to explain the connection between Jacob's obedience and Esau's actions?
options: To show that Esau's motivation was negative—he wanted to improve his standing after seeing Jacob succeed
To prove that Jacob was more righteous than Esau
To demonstrate that all the patriarchs were equally successful
points.kasha: The text doesn't explicitly state why Esau suddenly decided to marry someone from Ishmael's family at this moment.
points.answer: Rashi connects the events to show Esau's negative motivation: seeing Jacob receive the blessing and obey their father by going to Padan-aram, Esau wants to do something to gain favor, so he also takes a wife—though from a different family line.

points.q: What key historical information does Rashi derive from the seemingly redundant phrase 'sister of Nebaioth'?
options: That Ishmael died before Mahalath's marriage, and her brother Nebaioth conducted the ceremony
That Nebaioth was more important than Ishmael in Ishmael's family
That Mahalath had a special spiritual connection to her brother
points.kasha: The text calls her 'daughter of Ishmael' so why add 'sister of Nebaioth'—isn't that already implied?
points.answer: Rashi explains that this phrase teaches us Ishmael died after betrothing her to Esau but before the wedding, so her brother Nebaioth gave her away in marriage instead.

points.q: According to Rashi's calculation, what did Jacob do during the fourteen years not accounted for in his stated lifespan?
options: He studied Torah in Eber's School rather than going directly to Laban
He worked as a shepherd in his father's fields
He lived in hiding to escape Esau's anger
points.kasha: Jacob told Pharaoh he was 130 years old, but calculating his known years (14 with Laban before Joseph's birth, 30 years of Joseph before becoming ruler, 9 years until Jacob reached Egypt) from when he left his father leaves 14 years unaccounted for.
points.answer: Rashi deduces that Jacob spent fourteen years studying Torah in Eber's School on his way to Laban, and because of the merit of studying Torah, he received no punishment for this separation from his father.

points.q: What does Rashi criticize about Esau's action of taking an additional wife?
options: He compounded his wickedness by not divorcing his first wives before taking another
He was disrespectful to his first wives by choosing a wife from Ishmael's line
He performed the marriage ceremony incorrectly
points.kasha: The phrase 'besides his wives' could mean he simply added to his household, but Rashi seems to find something wrong with this action.
points.answer: Rashi teaches that Esau added wickedness to wickedness because he did not divorce his first wives before taking Mahalath as an additional wife.
